body_html:
How to think about it

The Earth rotates on its axis from west to east once in about 24 hours, giving day and night, and revolves round the Sun once in about 365¼ days. Its axis is tilted by about 23.5°, so each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight and longer days for part of the year: these are the seasons.

The Moon goes round the Earth, and we see different amounts of its sunlit half: the phases, from new moon to full moon and back in about 29.5 days. When the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth, there is a solar eclipse (on a new moon day); when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon, there is a lunar eclipse (on a full moon night).

Example

Which phase comes after the first quarter?

the lit part keeps growing

Answer: waxing gibbous

Example

June in India: season in Australia?

opposite hemisphere

Answer: winter

Common mistakes

  • Thinking seasons come from changing distance to the Sun.
  • Mixing up solar and lunar eclipses.
  • Thinking the Earth's shadow causes the phases.

faq.a: Because the Earth's axis is tilted, so as it revolves, each hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun for part of the year.

faq.q: When can a solar eclipse happen?
faq.a: Only on a new moon day, when the Moon is between the Sun and the Earth.

items.q: What do we call the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon?
items.e: A full moon: the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon.

items.q: Which of these is caused by the Earth's revolution with its tilted axis?
c: shadows changing direction from morning to evening
a place facing the Sun having daytime
stars appearing to move across the night sky in a few hours
items.e: The seasons: caused by the Earth's revolution with its tilted axis.

items.q: Which of these is not caused by the Earth's rotation?
c: the change in the length of shadows at noon over the year
a place facing the Sun having daytime
the Sun appearing to rise in the east and set in the west
items.e: The change in the length of shadows at noon over the year: not caused by the Earth's rotation. The other three are.

items.q: When it is summer in India (June), which season is it in Australia?
items.e: The southern hemisphere is tilted away then.

items.q: What is rotation?
c: the path of the Earth around the Sun or the Moon around the Earth
the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light
the Earth spinning on its axis once in about 24 hours
the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see
items.e: Rotation: the Earth spinning on its axis once in about 24 hours.

items.q: What is a solar eclipse?
c: the phase when the Moon's lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it
the Earth spinning on its axis once in about 24 hours
the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light
an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth
items.e: A solar eclipse: the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light.

items.q: How long does a total solar eclipse last at one place?
items.e: The Moon's shadow moves fast over the Earth.

items.q: What is the shape of the Earth's orbit around the Sun?
items.e: It is an ellipse that is almost a circle.

items.q: Why are days longer in summer?
c: the Sun is bigger in summer
our hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun
items.e: Nights are longer in winter.

items.q: What is a solstice?
c: the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light
a day when the day is the longest or the shortest of the year
the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon
the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see
items.e: A solstice: a day when the day is the longest or the shortest of the year.

items.q: What is the Tropic of Capricorn?
c: the line of latitude at about 23.5° S where the Sun is overhead at noon around 22 December
items.e: It passes through Australia and Brazil.

items.q: Why do we see phases of the Moon?
c: the Earth's shadow covers it each night
we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it moves round the Earth
items.e: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun.

items.q: Which of these is caused by the Earth's rotation?
c: the noon Sun being higher in summer than in winter
the change in the length of shadows at noon over the year
stars appearing to move across the night sky in a few hours
items.e: Stars appearing to move across the night sky in a few hours: caused by the Earth's rotation.

items.q: What is the Tropic of Cancer?
c: the line of latitude at about 23.5° N where the Sun is overhead at noon around 21 June
items.e: It passes through India.

items.q: What is a 'waxing' Moon?
c: the lit part we see is growing night by night
items.e: Waning means shrinking.

items.q: Which of these is not caused by the Earth's rotation?
c: stars appearing to move across the night sky in a few hours
a place facing the Sun having daytime
the Sun appearing to rise in the east and set in the west
items.e: The seasons: not caused by the Earth's rotation. The other three are.

items.q: What is the axis?
c: the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light
the Earth coming between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
the Earth going round the Sun once in about 365¼ days
an imaginary line through the North and South Poles about which the Earth spins
items.e: The axis: an imaginary line through the North and South Poles about which the Earth spins.

items.q: What do we call the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see?
items.e: The phases of the Moon: the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see.

items.q: What is an orbit?
c: an imaginary line through the North and South Poles about which the Earth spins
the path of the Earth around the Sun or the Moon around the Earth
an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth
the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon
items.e: An orbit: the path of the Earth around the Sun or the Moon around the Earth.

items.q: What is a lunar eclipse?
c: the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see
the Earth coming between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
a day when day and night are nearly equal everywhere
the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon
items.e: A lunar eclipse: the Earth coming between the Sun and the Moon, so the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

items.q: In June, the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun. Which season is it in New Zealand?
items.e: New Zealand is in the southern hemisphere, which is tilted away from the Sun in June.

items.q: In December, the North Pole is tilted away from the Sun. Which season is it in Argentina?
items.e: Argentina is in the southern hemisphere, which is tilted towards the Sun in December.

items.q: What is a lunar eclipse sometimes called when the Moon looks red?
items.e: Sunlight bent by the Earth's air reaches it.

items.q: What causes the seasons?
c: the changing distance of the Moon
the tilt of the Earth's axis as it goes round the Sun
items.e: Places get more direct sunlight in summer.

items.q: In which direction does the Earth rotate?
items.e: So the Sun seems to rise in the east.

items.q: In December, the North Pole is tilted away from the Sun. Which season is it in the United Kingdom?
items.e: The United Kingdom is in the northern hemisphere, which is tilted away from the Sun in December.

items.q: In December, the North Pole is tilted away from the Sun. Which season is it in Egypt?
items.e: Egypt is in the northern hemisphere, which is tilted away from the Sun in December.

items.q: How long does the Moon take to go from one full moon to the next?
items.e: This is the basis of many calendars.

items.q: In June, the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun. Which season is it in Japan?
items.e: Japan is in the northern hemisphere, which is tilted towards the Sun in June.

items.q: What would happen if the Earth stopped rotating?

items.e: Rotation gives day and night.

items.q: Why are there no seasons on the Moon like on Earth?
c: it is too small to be seen

items.e: Its days and nights are about two weeks long.

items.q: In June, the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun. Which season is it in Argentina?
items.e: Argentina is in the southern hemisphere, which is tilted away from the Sun in June.

items.q: What is the Moon?
items.e: It has no light of its own.

items.q: In June, the North Pole is tilted towards the Sun. Which season is it in Egypt?
items.e: Egypt is in the northern hemisphere, which is tilted towards the Sun in June.

items.q: Which line of latitude divides the Earth into the northern and southern hemispheres?
items.e: India is in the northern hemisphere.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just after the first quarter?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the full moon?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Why does a lunar eclipse not happen every full moon?
c: the Moon's orbit is slightly tilted, so it usually passes above or below the Earth's shadow
items.e: Eclipses happen only when they line up.

items.q: What do we call an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth?
items.e: The equator: an imaginary line around the middle of the Earth.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: What do we call a day when the day is the longest or the shortest of the year?
items.e: A solstice: a day when the day is the longest or the shortest of the year.

items.q: Why does the Sun appear to rise in the east?
c: the Sun moves from east to west
the Earth rotates from west to east
items.e: The stars seem to move the same way.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waning crescent?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the waxing gibbous?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the last quarter?
items.e: The order is new moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent → new moon.

items.q: Why are the polar regions cold even in their summer?
c: they are closest to the Sun
the Sun's rays fall on them at a very slant angle
items.e: They get months of daylight in summer.

items.q: What is a new moon?

the Earth going round the Sun once in about 365¼ days
a day when the day is the longest or the shortest of the year

items.e: A new moon: the phase when the Moon's lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it.

items.q: What do we call the path of the Earth around the Sun or the Moon around the Earth?
items.e: An orbit: the path of the Earth around the Sun or the Moon around the Earth.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon is seen when the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun?
items.e: Its whole lit side faces us.

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just after the waning gibbous?

items.q: Which phase of the Moon comes just before the first quarter?

items.q: What is a full moon?
c: the changing shapes of the lit part of the Moon that we see
the phase when the Moon's lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it
the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light

items.e: A full moon: the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon.

items.q: What do we call an imaginary line through the North and South Poles about which the Earth spins?

items.q: Which of these is true of a solar eclipse?
c: the sky can turn dark during the day
the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon
items.e: The sky can turn dark during the day: true of a solar eclipse.

items.q: Which of these is true of a lunar eclipse?
c: the sky can turn dark during the day
it is seen only from a narrow strip of the Earth at a time
it can happen only on a full moon night
it must never be watched with the naked eye
items.e: It can happen only on a full moon night: true of a lunar eclipse.

items.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
c: it takes the same time to spin once as to go round the Earth once
the Earth hides the other side
items.e: The far side was first photographed by spacecraft.

items.q: Which of these is not true of a lunar eclipse?
c: it can happen only on a new moon day
the Earth is between the Sun and the Moon
it can be seen from the whole night side of the Earth
it can happen only on a full moon night
items.e: It can happen only on a new moon day: not true of a lunar eclipse. The other three are.

items.q: Why is it hotter at noon than in the early morning?
c: the Sun's rays fall more directly at noon
the Moon is far at noon
the Sun is closer at noon
items.e: Slanting rays spread their heat.

items.q: What do we call the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light?
items.e: A solar eclipse: the Moon coming between the Sun and the Earth, blocking the Sun's light.

items.q: What is an equinox?
c: an imaginary line through the North and South Poles about which the Earth spins
the path of the Earth around the Sun or the Moon around the Earth
a day when day and night are nearly equal everywhere
the phase when we see the whole lit face of the Moon
items.e: An equinox: a day when day and night are nearly equal everywhere.

items.q: What do we call the phase when the Moon's lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it?
items.e: A new moon: the phase when the Moon's lit side faces away from us and we cannot see it.

items.q: Why should we never look directly at the Sun during a solar eclipse?
c: it is too dark to see
the strong light can damage our eyes

items.q: Which of these is true of a lunar eclipse?

items.q: Why does the Moon rise about 50 minutes later each day?

items.e: It takes about a month to go round.
